title: 2 Chronicles 18:1–11
context: 2 Chronicles 18 parallels 1 Kings 22:1–35, the Micaiah scene and the battle at Ramoth Gilead. Chronicles opens by saying that Jehoshaphat, having riches and honor in abundance, “allied himself with Ahab” (18:1). The WEB does not specify the kind of alliance; the verb is often understood of a marriage alliance, which fits the later note that Jehoshaphat’s son Jehoram “had Ahab’s daughter as his wife” (21:6). Chronicles adds that Ahab killed sheep and cattle in abundance and “moved him to go up with him” (18:2), and it lacks the three years without war and Ahab’s complaint to his servants (1 Kings 22:1–3). Wording differences are named rather than harmonized, such as the prophets’ answer “Go up, for God will deliver it into the hand of the king” (18:5), where Kings has “the Lord.” Both traditions read the scene as shared ground on the danger of seeking only welcome counsel, consistent with the notes on 1 Kings 22:1–12.

verses.text: Now Jehoshaphat had riches and honor in abundance; and he allied himself with Ahab.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoshaphat, who has riches and honor in abundance, allies himself with Ahab. The verb is often understood of a marriage alliance, which fits 21:6, where Jehoram is married to Ahab’s daughter; the WEB itself says only that he allied himself.

Arminian readers see a real choice by a prosperous king, made freely, with consequences the following chapters will show.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the Chronicler sets the alliance directly after the account of God’s blessing, and they see in it the danger that prosperity can lead even a godly king to unwise partnerships, a judgment made explicit in 19:2.

Both traditions read the alliance as a serious misstep by a faithful king and treat the verse as shared ground, consistent with the notes on 1 Kings 22:2.

verses.text: After some years, he went down to Ahab to Samaria. Ahab killed sheep and cattle for him in abundance, and for the people who were with him, and moved him to go up with him to Ramoth Gilead.
verses.arminianNotes:
After some years Jehoshaphat goes down to Ahab in Samaria, and Ahab kills sheep and cattle in abundance for him and his people and “moved him to go up with him to Ramoth Gilead”. Kings does not record the feast.

Arminian readers note the persuasion involved, and they see Ahab’s hospitality as pressure on Jehoshaphat’s freedom rather than a removal of it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the same English verb, moved, appears again in 18:31, where God moves the Syrian captains away, and they see a contrast between Ahab’s moving of Jehoshaphat into danger and God’s moving of his enemies to spare him.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the influence of ungodly allies and the need for discernment.

verses.text: Ahab king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat king of Judah, “Will you go with me to Ramoth Gilead?” He answered him, “I am as you are, and my people as your people. We will be with you in the war.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Ahab asks Jehoshaphat to go with him to Ramoth Gilead, and Jehoshaphat answers, “I am as you are, and my people as your people. We will be with you in the war.” Kings has “my horses as your horses” instead of the last sentence.

Arminian readers note the sweeping commitment Jehoshaphat makes before any word from the LORD has been sought.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a close identification with Ahab that the narrative will test, and they note, as the notes on 1 Kings 22:4 do, that loyalty to an ally is not wrong in itself but is given here too quickly.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: even a faithful king can commit himself to a partner whose way is not the LORD’s before asking what the LORD wants.

verses.text: Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, “Please inquire first for the LORD’s word.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoshaphat says to the king of Israel, “Please inquire first for the LORD’s word.” The wording matches Kings.

Arminian readers note that Jehoshaphat genuinely wants God’s guidance, even though he has already promised his support, and they see in the request a heart that still looks to the LORD despite his haste.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also commend the request, while noting that it comes after the commitment rather than before it, so that the rest of the chapter tests whether the word will actually be heeded once it is given.

Both traditions agree that seeking the LORD’s word is right, and they treat the verse as shared ground consistent with the notes on 1 Kings 22:5.

verses.text: Then the king of Israel gathered the prophets together, four hundred men, and said to them, “Shall we go to Ramoth Gilead to battle, or shall I forbear?” They said, “Go up, for God will deliver it into the hand of the king.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The king of Israel gathers four hundred prophets and asks whether to go to battle or forbear, and they answer, “Go up, for God will deliver it into the hand of the king.” Kings has “about four hundred men” and “Go up; for the Lord will deliver it into the hand of the king”.

Arminian readers note the unanimity, which does not reassure Jehoshaphat.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see prophets who tell the king what he wants to hear, and they note that the promise does not specify which king, an ambiguity that later events expose.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: agreement among many voices is not the same as a true word from the LORD, and the wording differences from Kings are recorded without being harmonized.

verses.text: But Jehoshaphat said, “Isn’t there here a prophet of the LORD besides, that we may inquire of him?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoshaphat asks whether there is not a prophet of the LORD besides these, so that they may inquire of him. He is not satisfied with the four hundred.

Arminian readers note his discernment and see a king who senses that something is missing, a sign that the habit of seeking the LORD shapes his judgment even in a compromised setting.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see godly discernment at work, and they note that the question implies the four hundred have not clearly spoken as the LORD’s messengers, which prepares for the arrival of Micaiah.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground on testing what claims to be a word from God, consistent with the notes on 1 Kings 22:7.

verses.text: The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “There is yet one man by whom we may inquire of the LORD; but I hate him, for he never prophesies good concerning me, but always evil. He is Micaiah the son of Imla.” Jehoshaphat said, “Don’t let the king say so.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Ahab says there is one man, Micaiah son of Imla, but “I hate him, for he never prophesies good concerning me, but always evil”, and Jehoshaphat answers, “Don’t let the king say so.” Kings spells the name Imlah and has “he does not prophesy good concerning me, but evil”.

Arminian readers note that Ahab judges a prophet by whether he likes the message.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see in Ahab’s words a heart set against unwelcome truth, and they note that Chronicles’ stronger wording, never and always, sharpens Ahab’s complaint.

Both traditions agree on the pastoral point: hating a messenger because the message is hard is a danger for every hearer, not only for kings.

verses.text: Then the king of Israel called an officer, and said, “Get Micaiah the son of Imla quickly.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The king of Israel calls an officer and says, “Get Micaiah the son of Imla quickly.” The true word is sent for.

Arminian readers note that Ahab yields to Jehoshaphat’s request, though reluctantly, and they see the opportunity to hear God’s word given even to a king who does not want it, so that he will be without excuse.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the LORD’s providence bringing his prophet before the king despite Ahab’s dislike, and they note that God’s word reaches those who resist it as well as those who welcome it.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, consistent with the notes on 1 Kings 22:9: God’s word reaches Ahab, and he is responsible for his response.

verses.text: Now the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah each sat on his throne, arrayed in their robes, and they were sitting in an open place at the entrance of the gate of Samaria; and all the prophets were prophesying before them.
verses.arminianNotes:
The two kings sit on their thrones, arrayed in their robes, in an open place at the entrance of the gate of Samaria, while all the prophets prophesy before them. The wording is very close to Kings.

Arminian readers note the public, royal setting, which adds pressure on everyone present to conform to the majority and makes dissent costly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the contrast between the two kings’ thrones and the heavenly throne Micaiah will describe in 18:18, and they note that earthly splendor does not determine what will happen at Ramoth Gilead.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: earthly power, however impressive, sits under the LORD’s rule.

verses.text: Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah made himself horns of iron and said, “The LORD says, ‘With these you shall push the Syrians, until they are consumed.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
Zedekiah son of Chenaanah makes horns of iron and claims to speak for the LORD, saying that with these the king will push the Syrians until they are consumed. The sign-act is dramatic.

Arminian readers note that he invokes the LORD’s name directly, and that using the right words does not make a message true, so hearers must test what they are told.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a sign-act that appears convincing but is not from the LORD, and they note the law’s warning against speaking in God’s name what he has not commanded (Deuteronomy 18:20).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: speaking in the LORD’s name carries great responsibility, consistent with the notes on 1 Kings 22:11.

verses.text: All the prophets prophesied so, saying, “Go up to Ramoth Gilead, and prosper; for the LORD will deliver it into the hand of the king.”
verses.arminianNotes:
All the prophets prophesy, “Go up to Ramoth Gilead, and prosper; for the LORD will deliver it into the hand of the king.” The message now uses the divine name.

Arminian readers note that the chorus grows louder but not more reliable, and they see the pressure of a united voice urging the kings forward as a test of whether they will wait for a true word.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the use of the LORD’s name does not make the prophecy true, and they see the scene as preparing for the disclosure in 18:22 of what lies behind the prophets’ agreement.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: truth is not settled by majority, and the reader is about to hear a different word.
